vocabulary.definition: A molecule with an uneven charge distribution caused by unequal sharing of electrons.
An atom’s relative ability to attract shared electrons in a covalent bond.
A weak attraction between a partially positive hydrogen atom and a nearby electronegative atom.
Attraction between molecules of the same substance, as occurs between water molecules.
Attraction between molecules of different substances, such as water and a vessel wall.
Resistance of a liquid surface to deformation because its surface molecules attract one another.
Movement of liquid through a narrow space produced by adhesion, cohesion, and surface tension.
The dissolving medium in a solution; water fills this role in most cells.
A substance dissolved and uniformly dispersed within a solvent.
A homogeneous mixture in which water is the dissolving medium.
Describes a charged or polar substance that interacts readily with water.
Describes a non-polar substance that does not interact favorably with water.
Energy required to raise the temperature of a unit mass of substance by one degree.
Energy required to convert a unit mass of liquid to gas without changing temperature.
An open hydrogen-bonded arrangement that makes solid water less dense than liquid water.
A nucleic-acid monomer containing a pentose sugar, a phosphate group, and a nitrogenous base.
A nitrogenous base joined to a pentose sugar, with no phosphate group attached.
The five-carbon sugar in DNA, lacking an oxygen atom at its 2′ carbon.
The five-carbon sugar in RNA, with hydroxyl groups at both the 2′ and 3′ carbons.
A double-ring nitrogenous base; adenine and guanine belong to this class.
A single-ring nitrogenous base; cytosine, thymine, and uracil belong to this class.
A covalent link joining the phosphate of one nucleotide to sugars in adjacent nucleotides.
The alternating covalently bonded sugars and phosphates forming the structural framework of a nucleic-acid strand.
Two nucleic-acid strands aligned in opposite 5′-to-3′ directions.
Specific hydrogen bonding of adenine with thymine or uracil, and guanine with cytosine.
Two antiparallel polynucleotide strands wound around a common axis and held together by base pairing.
A usually double-stranded nucleic acid that stores hereditary information in its base sequence.
A usually single-stranded nucleic acid used in gene expression and some catalytic or regulatory roles.
The end of a nucleic-acid strand bearing a phosphate associated with the sugar’s 5′ carbon.
The end of a nucleic-acid strand bearing a free hydroxyl group on the sugar’s 3′ carbon.
The natural emergence of living systems from non-living chemical components on early Earth.
Chemical processes before life that could produce and organize biologically useful molecules.
The disproven claim that complex living organisms routinely arise from non-living matter.
The principle that new living organisms arise from pre-existing living organisms.
A simulation of proposed early-Earth conditions that produced amino acids from simple gases and energy.
A non-living, membrane-bounded chemical system with some properties associated with cells.
A closed, water-filled compartment enclosed by a self-assembled lipid bilayer.
Production of a copy by using the original structure or sequence as a template.
A reaction in which a product increases the rate of its own formation.
The proposal that early life used RNA for both information storage and chemical catalysis.
An RNA molecule that catalyzes a chemical reaction.
The ancestral population from which all currently living organisms ultimately descend.
The proposal that mineral-rich seafloor vents supplied gradients and surfaces that promoted life’s origin.
A chemical setting that favors electron gain and contains little free molecular oxygen.
The explanation that mitochondria and chloroplasts evolved from bacteria engulfed by an ancestral host cell.
The principles that organisms consist of cells, cells are life’s basic units, and cells arise from existing cells.
A cell lacking a membrane-bound nucleus and other membrane-bound organelles.
A cell with DNA enclosed in a nucleus and with membrane-bound organelles.
The selectively permeable boundary separating a cell’s contents from its external environment.
The aqueous part of the cytoplasm outside membrane-bound organelles.
The non-membrane-bound region of a prokaryotic cell containing its main chromosome.
A small, independently replicating DNA molecule separate from the main bacterial chromosome.
A mesh-like polymer of sugars and peptides that strengthens most bacterial cell walls.
A complex of ribosomal RNA and proteins that translates messenger RNA into a polypeptide.
The smaller ribosome type found in prokaryotes, mitochondria, and chloroplasts, containing 50S and 30S subunits.
The larger ribosome type in the eukaryotic cytosol, containing 60S and 40S subunits.
An instrument that uses electrons rather than visible light to resolve very small cellular structures.
The ratio of an image’s measured size to the specimen’s actual size.
The ability to distinguish two nearby points as separate structures.
A line on an image that represents a stated actual distance in the specimen.
An acellular infectious agent consisting of genetic material in a protein coat, sometimes surrounded by an envelope.
vocabulary.sourceTitle: OpenStax Biology 2e, 21.1 Viral Evolution, Morphology, and Classification

vocabulary.definition: A complete virus particle outside a host cell and capable of initiating infection.
vocabulary.sourceTitle: OpenStax Biology 2e, 21.1 Viral Evolution, Morphology, and Classification

vocabulary.definition: The protein shell that encloses and protects a virus’s genetic material.
vocabulary.sourceTitle: OpenStax Biology 2e, 21.1 Viral Evolution, Morphology, and Classification

vocabulary.definition: A repeating protein subunit that assembles with others to form a capsid.
vocabulary.sourceTitle: OpenStax Biology 2e, 21.1 Viral Evolution, Morphology, and Classification

vocabulary.definition: A host-derived lipid membrane surrounding some virions and bearing virus-encoded proteins.
vocabulary.sourceTitle: OpenStax Biology 2e, 21.1 Viral Evolution, Morphology, and Classification

vocabulary.definition: The DNA or RNA sequence carrying the hereditary information of a virus.
vocabulary.sourceTitle: OpenStax Biology 2e, 21.1 Viral Evolution, Morphology, and Classification

vocabulary.definition: The set of host species or cell types that a virus can infect.
vocabulary.sourceTitle: OpenStax Biology 2e, 21.1 Viral Evolution, Morphology, and Classification

vocabulary.definition: An agent that can reproduce only by using the machinery of a living host cell.
vocabulary.sourceTitle: OpenStax Biology 2e, 21.1 Viral Evolution, Morphology, and Classification

vocabulary.definition: A virus that infects bacteria.
vocabulary.sourceTitle: OpenStax Biology 2e, 21.1 Viral Evolution, Morphology, and Classification

vocabulary.definition: Viral replication that rapidly produces virions and usually ends with rupture of the host cell.
vocabulary.sourceTitle: OpenStax Biology 2e, 21.1 Viral Evolution, Morphology, and Classification

vocabulary.definition: A bacteriophage pathway in which viral DNA persists in a host genome before possible activation.
vocabulary.sourceTitle: OpenStax Biology 2e, 21.1 Viral Evolution, Morphology, and Classification

vocabulary.definition: Bacteriophage DNA integrated into a bacterial chromosome during lysogeny.
vocabulary.sourceTitle: OpenStax Biology 2e, 21.1 Viral Evolution, Morphology, and Classification

vocabulary.definition: An RNA virus that makes a DNA copy of its genome inside the host cell.
vocabulary.sourceTitle: OpenStax Biology 2e, 21.1 Viral Evolution, Morphology, and Classification

vocabulary.definition: An enzyme that synthesizes DNA using RNA as the template.
vocabulary.sourceTitle: OpenStax Biology 2e, 21.1 Viral Evolution, Morphology, and Classification

vocabulary.definition: Viral DNA integrated into the chromosome of a eukaryotic host cell.
vocabulary.sourceTitle: OpenStax Biology 2e, 21.1 Viral Evolution, Morphology, and Classification

vocabulary.definition: A species definition based on natural interbreeding and reproductive isolation from other groups.
A species definition based on a consistent set of observable structural features.
The two-part scientific naming system that combines a genus name with a specific epithet.
A taxonomic rank above species whose name forms the first part of a binomial.
The second, lowercase part of a species’ scientific binomial; it is not a complete name alone.
The broadest commonly used taxonomic rank, above kingdom.
The domain of prokaryotes whose cell walls usually contain peptidoglycan.
The domain of prokaryotes distinct from bacteria in membrane chemistry and many genetic features.
The domain containing organisms whose cells have nuclei and membrane-bound organelles.
An identification tool that narrows possibilities through a sequence of paired alternatives.
A non-vascular land plant such as a moss, liverwort, or hornwort.
A seedless vascular plant that produces spores, typically on fronds.
A vascular seed plant whose ovules and seeds are not enclosed within an ovary.
A flowering plant whose seeds develop within an ovary that matures into a fruit.
A chordate animal with a vertebral column surrounding the spinal cord.
The science of naming, describing, and classifying organisms.
A named group of organisms at any rank in a classification system.
A common ancestor together with all of its descendants.
A branching diagram representing hypothesized relationships based on shared derived characteristics.
A branch point on a phylogenetic tree representing a common ancestor or lineage split.
A shared derived characteristic used as evidence that taxa belong to the same clade.
A comparison taxon outside the group being studied, used to identify ancestral character states.
A grouping that contains an ancestor but excludes one or more descendant lineages.
A grouping assembled from separate lineages while excluding their most recent common ancestor.
A method that estimates divergence time from an assumed rate of sequence change.
Arrangement of DNA, RNA, or protein sequences to identify corresponding positions and differences.
The criterion favoring the phylogenetic explanation requiring the fewest evolutionary changes.
The evolutionary history and relationships of a species or group of species.
Two lineages that share an immediate common ancestor not shared with any other lineage.
Change in the inherited characteristics of populations across generations.
The proportion of all copies of a gene in a population represented by a particular allele.
All alleles present in the reproductive members of a population at a given time.
A change in allele frequencies within a population over relatively short evolutionary time.
The evolutionary formation of new species through divergence and reproductive isolation.
Barriers that prevent gene flow between populations by stopping mating or fertile offspring production.
A reproductive obstacle that prevents mating or fertilization before a zygote forms.
A reproductive obstacle that reduces the survival or fertility of hybrid offspring after fertilization.
Formation of species after geographic separation interrupts gene flow between populations.
Formation of species without geographic separation, often through ecological or chromosomal isolation.
Rapid diversification of one ancestral lineage into species adapted to different ecological roles.
Accumulation of differences between related lineages exposed to different selection pressures.
Independent evolution of similar features in distantly related lineages under similar selection pressures.
A feature shared because of common ancestry, even if its current functions differ.
A feature with a similar function in different lineages but an independent evolutionary origin.
The variety of life at genetic, species, and ecosystem levels.
Variation in alleles and genotypes within a species or population.
The combined richness and relative abundance of species in a community.
Variation among habitats, biological communities, and ecological processes within a region.
A species naturally restricted to a particular geographic area.
A species assessed as vulnerable, endangered, or critically endangered under the IUCN categories.
The permanent loss of a species when its final living individual dies.
Protection of species in their natural habitats and ecological communities.
Protection of biological diversity outside natural habitats, such as in seed banks or zoos.
A geographically defined region managed to achieve long-term conservation of nature.
Managed reproduction outside the wild intended to maintain genetic diversity and support recovery.
A controlled collection that stores viable seeds to conserve plant genetic diversity.
A species whose ecological effect is disproportionately large relative to its abundance.
A species whose presence, absence, or condition reveals information about environmental quality.
The science and practice of assisting recovery of damaged, degraded, or destroyed ecosystems.
A single sugar unit that cannot be hydrolyzed into a simpler carbohydrate.
A six-carbon monosaccharide used widely as a respiratory substrate and building block.
A carbohydrate formed when two monosaccharides are joined by a glycosidic bond.
A polymer composed of many monosaccharides linked by glycosidic bonds.
A reaction that forms a covalent bond between molecules while releasing water.
Cleavage of a covalent bond by adding the components of water.
A covalent linkage joining one sugar residue to another group, commonly another sugar.
A plant glucose-storage polymer composed of amylose and branched amylopectin.
A highly branched glucose-storage polymer found mainly in animals and fungi.
An unbranched polymer of β-glucose whose hydrogen-bonded microfibrils strengthen plant cell walls.
A lipid formed from glycerol joined by ester bonds to three fatty acids.
A hydrocarbon chain with a terminal carboxyl group and variable chain length or unsaturation.
A fatty acid containing no carbon–carbon double bonds in its hydrocarbon chain.
A fatty acid containing one or more carbon–carbon double bonds in its hydrocarbon chain.
An amphipathic lipid with a phosphate-containing head and two hydrophobic fatty-acid tails.
A protein monomer with amino and carboxyl groups bonded to a central carbon bearing a variable side chain.
The variable side chain that determines an amino acid’s chemical properties.
The covalent amide linkage formed between the carboxyl group of one amino acid and another’s amino group.
A linear chain of amino-acid residues joined by peptide bonds.
The specific linear sequence of amino acids in a polypeptide.
Local backbone folding stabilized by hydrogen bonds, especially α-helices and β-pleated sheets.
The overall three-dimensional shape of one polypeptide produced by interactions among side chains and the backbone.
The arrangement and interaction of multiple polypeptide subunits in one functional protein.
A coiled secondary structure stabilized by hydrogen bonds within the polypeptide backbone.
A sheet-like secondary structure stabilized by hydrogen bonds between adjacent backbone segments.
A covalent bond between the sulfur atoms of two cysteine side chains.
Loss of a protein’s native shape and function without necessarily breaking its peptide bonds.
A compact, generally soluble protein whose folded shape supports roles such as catalysis or transport.
An elongated, usually insoluble protein specialized for structural or mechanical functions.
A protein associated with a non-protein component required for its biological function.
A model describing membranes as mobile lipids containing a changing mosaic of proteins and other components.
Two layers of phospholipids with hydrophobic tails inward and hydrophilic heads facing surrounding water.
Having both hydrophilic and hydrophobic regions within the same molecule.
A protein permanently embedded in the lipid bilayer, often spanning it completely.
A protein loosely attached to a membrane surface or to another membrane protein.
An animal-membrane steroid that buffers fluidity and reduces permeability to small polar molecules.
A protein with covalently attached carbohydrate chains used in recognition, adhesion, or signaling.
A membrane lipid with an attached carbohydrate that contributes to cell recognition and membrane stability.
The property of allowing some substances to cross a membrane more readily than others.
Net movement down a concentration gradient directly through a membrane without a transport protein.
Passive movement down an electrochemical gradient through a channel or carrier protein.
A membrane protein forming a hydrophilic pore through which selected particles can pass.
A membrane protein that binds a solute and changes shape to move it across the bilayer.
Movement against an electrochemical gradient using energy and a specific membrane protein.
Bulk entry into a cell by invagination of the plasma membrane and formation of a vesicle.
Bulk export from a cell when an internal vesicle fuses with the plasma membrane.
A double-membrane organelle containing most of a eukaryotic cell’s genetic material.
A double membrane with nuclear pores that regulates exchange between the nucleus and cytoplasm.
A nuclear region where ribosomal RNA is transcribed and ribosomal subunits begin assembly.
A membrane network bearing ribosomes that synthesizes and begins processing secreted or membrane proteins.
A ribosome-free membrane network involved in lipid synthesis, detoxification, and calcium storage.
Stacks of membranes that modify, sort, and package proteins and lipids into vesicles.
An acidic, enzyme-filled organelle that digests macromolecules and worn cellular components.
An organelle that oxidizes selected molecules and breaks down hydrogen peroxide using catalase.
A double-membrane organelle where aerobic respiration produces most cellular ATP.
A photosynthetic organelle in plants and algae containing thylakoids, stroma, and its own DNA.
A cylindrical microtubule structure involved in organizing animal-cell spindle microtubules and basal bodies.
A small membrane-bound compartment that moves materials between organelles or the plasma membrane.
A large plant-cell compartment that stores solutes and helps maintain turgor pressure.
A dynamic network of protein filaments that supports cell shape, transport, division, and movement.
Interconnected or vesicle-linked membranes that synthesize, modify, and transport cell products.
Separation of cellular processes into distinct regions, allowing specialized and independently regulated conditions.
Development of distinct cell structures and functions through regulated changes in gene activity.
An unspecialized cell able to self-renew and produce one or more differentiated cell types.
Able to generate every cell type of an organism, including extraembryonic tissues.
Able to generate nearly any body cell type but not an entire organism with supporting tissues.
Able to generate several related cell types within a particular tissue or lineage.
A size relationship that generally decreases as a cell grows, limiting exchange across its boundary.
A red blood cell specialized for gas transport by its biconcave shape and high hemoglobin content.
A motile male gamete specialized to deliver a haploid nucleus to an egg.
A developing female germ cell that can mature into an ovum.
An excitable cell specialized to receive, process, and transmit electrical and chemical signals.
A long multinucleate cell packed with contractile myofibrils for voluntary movement.
A chloroplast-rich leaf cell specialized for light absorption and photosynthesis.
A root epidermal cell with a long projection that increases mineral-ion and water uptake.
A lignified dead cell joined end-to-end to conduct water and provide support.
A living phloem cell that conducts assimilates through perforated end walls with companion-cell support.
Movement of respiratory gases between an organism and its environment across a specialized surface.
Bulk movement of air or water that renews the medium at a respiratory surface.
A difference in one gas’s pressure that drives its net diffusion.
A microscopic lung air sac providing a thin, moist surface closely associated with capillaries.
A thin alveolar epithelial cell forming most of the surface across which gases diffuse.
An alveolar epithelial cell that secretes surfactant and can replace damaged alveolar cells.
A phospholipid-rich secretion that reduces alveolar surface tension and helps prevent collapse.
A dome-shaped skeletal muscle whose contraction increases thoracic volume during inhalation.
The volume of air inhaled or exhaled in one normal resting breath.
The greatest volume exhaled after the deepest possible inhalation.
The number of ventilation cycles per unit time, commonly measured as breaths per minute.
A slender gill projection bearing many lamellae and supporting blood vessels.
A thin plate on a gill filament that provides a large surface for aquatic gas exchange.
Opposite flow of blood and water that maintains an oxygen gradient across an entire gill surface.
A regulated epidermal pore through which carbon dioxide, oxygen, and water vapor move in plants.
One of a pair of specialized epidermal cells that controls the opening of a stoma.
Collective movement of a fluid and its dissolved substances down a pressure gradient.
A transport system in which blood remains within vessels separate from interstitial fluid.
A blood vessel that carries blood away from the heart under relatively high pressure.
A blood vessel that carries blood toward the heart and commonly contains valves.
A microscopic, thin-walled vessel where materials exchange between blood and tissues.
The force per unit area exerted by circulating blood on vessel walls.
The repeating sequence of atrial and ventricular contraction and relaxation during one heartbeat.
The phase of a heart chamber’s cycle in which its muscle contracts.
The phase of a heart chamber’s cycle in which its muscle relaxes and the chamber fills.
A one-way valve between an atrium and ventricle that prevents backflow into the atrium.
A one-way valve at a ventricular outlet that prevents arterial blood returning to the ventricle.
The volume of blood pumped by one ventricle per minute, equal to heart rate times stroke volume.
An iron-containing tetrameric protein in red blood cells that reversibly binds oxygen.
Plant vascular tissue that conducts water and mineral ions and provides mechanical support.
Loss of water vapor from a plant, mainly by evaporation and diffusion through stomata.
The explanation that transpiration-generated tension pulls a cohesive water column upward through xylem.
Living vascular tissue that transports sucrose and other assimilates between plant sources and sinks.
Pressure-driven transport of organic assimilates through phloem sieve tubes.
A plant region that releases more assimilate into phloem than it consumes or stores.
A plant region that removes assimilate from phloem for use or storage.
Striated muscle attached to the skeleton and generally controlled voluntarily.
vocabulary.sourceTitle: OpenStax Biology 2e, 38.4 Muscle Contraction and Locomotion

vocabulary.definition: A contractile bundle within a muscle fiber composed of repeating sarcomeres.
vocabulary.sourceTitle: OpenStax Biology 2e, 38.4 Muscle Contraction and Locomotion

vocabulary.definition: The repeating contractile unit of a myofibril between two Z discs.
vocabulary.sourceTitle: OpenStax Biology 2e, 38.4 Muscle Contraction and Locomotion

vocabulary.definition: The main protein of thin filaments, bearing sites that interact with myosin heads.
vocabulary.sourceTitle: OpenStax Biology 2e, 38.4 Muscle Contraction and Locomotion

vocabulary.definition: A motor protein whose heads bind actin and use ATP to generate force.
vocabulary.sourceTitle: OpenStax Biology 2e, 38.4 Muscle Contraction and Locomotion

vocabulary.definition: A filament protein that covers myosin-binding sites on actin when skeletal muscle is relaxed.
vocabulary.sourceTitle: OpenStax Biology 2e, 38.4 Muscle Contraction and Locomotion

vocabulary.definition: A regulatory protein complex that binds calcium and shifts tropomyosin away from actin’s binding sites.
vocabulary.sourceTitle: OpenStax Biology 2e, 38.4 Muscle Contraction and Locomotion

vocabulary.definition: Contraction by movement of thin filaments past thick filaments, shortening sarcomeres without shortening either filament.
vocabulary.sourceTitle: OpenStax Biology 2e, 38.4 Muscle Contraction and Locomotion

vocabulary.definition: A temporary attachment between a myosin head and an actin filament during contraction.
vocabulary.sourceTitle: OpenStax Biology 2e, 38.4 Muscle Contraction and Locomotion

vocabulary.definition: The pivot of an actin-bound myosin head that pulls the thin filament toward the sarcomere center.
vocabulary.sourceTitle: OpenStax Biology 2e, 38.4 Muscle Contraction and Locomotion

vocabulary.definition: A nerve cell that transmits signals from the central nervous system to muscle fibers.
vocabulary.sourceTitle: OpenStax Biology 2e, 38.4 Muscle Contraction and Locomotion

vocabulary.definition: The chemical synapse between a motor neuron terminal and a skeletal muscle fiber.
vocabulary.sourceTitle: OpenStax Biology 2e, 38.4 Muscle Contraction and Locomotion

vocabulary.definition: The neurotransmitter released by motor neurons to depolarize skeletal muscle fibers.
vocabulary.sourceTitle: OpenStax Biology 2e, 38.4 Muscle Contraction and Locomotion

vocabulary.definition: A specialized smooth endoplasmic reticulum that stores and releases calcium in muscle fibers.
vocabulary.sourceTitle: OpenStax Biology 2e, 38.4 Muscle Contraction and Locomotion

vocabulary.definition: Two muscles that move a joint in opposite directions because one contracts as the other relaxes.
vocabulary.sourceTitle: OpenStax Biology 2e, 38.4 Muscle Contraction and Locomotion

vocabulary.definition: An inherited feature that increases reproductive success in a particular environment.
A reversible physiological adjustment by an individual in response to an environmental change.
An inherited anatomical feature that improves performance or survival in a particular environment.
An inherited functional process that improves performance or survival under particular conditions.
An inherited pattern of action that improves survival or reproductive success.
The ability of one genotype to produce different phenotypes under different environmental conditions.
A plant adapted to habitats where liquid water is scarce.
A plant adapted to living partly or wholly in water.
A plant adapted to grow in a highly saline environment.
Control of body temperature through physiological or behavioral mechanisms.
An animal whose body temperature depends mainly on external heat sources.
An animal that maintains substantial body heat through internally generated metabolism.
Material or tissue that reduces heat transfer between an organism and its environment.
Opposite flow of warm and cool blood that conserves heat by maintaining a transfer gradient.
Control of water balance and solute concentrations in body fluids.
A species’ multidimensional role, resource use, and tolerated conditions within an ecosystem.
The full range of conditions and resources a species could use without biotic constraints.
The conditions and resources a species actually uses after biotic interactions restrict it.
The physical place or environment in which an organism lives.
Division of limited resources among competing species through differences in use, place, or time.
The prediction that species with identical niches cannot coexist indefinitely when a shared resource is limiting.
Competition between individuals of different species for a limiting resource.
Competition among members of the same species for a limiting resource.
An interaction in which one organism kills and consumes another organism.
A close interaction in which both participating species gain a net benefit.
An interaction in which one species benefits while the other is neither significantly helped nor harmed.
An interaction in which a parasite benefits while reducing the fitness of its host.
A non-living physical or chemical component of an environment.
A living component or biological interaction that affects an organism.
The span of an environmental variable within which an organism can survive and reproduce.
An environmental resource or condition whose scarcity or excess restricts distribution, abundance, or growth.
The complete set of chemical reactions occurring in a cell or organism.
A sequence of energy-requiring reactions that builds complex molecules from simpler ones.
A sequence of reactions that breaks complex molecules into simpler ones and releases usable energy.
A biological catalyst that increases reaction rate without being consumed by the reaction.
The region of an enzyme where specific substrates bind and catalysis occurs.
A reactant molecule that binds to an enzyme and is chemically changed.
The temporary association formed when a substrate is bound in an enzyme’s active site.
The minimum energy input needed for reactants to reach a transition state.
The model in which substrate binding changes active-site shape to promote catalysis.
The selective recognition and catalysis of particular substrates or reactions by an enzyme.
Reduction of enzyme activity when an inhibitor competes with substrate for the active site.
Reduction of enzyme activity by inhibitor binding away from the active site, lowering catalytic capacity.
A regulatory binding site distinct from the active site that changes protein activity when occupied.
A non-protein ion or molecule required for the activity of some enzymes.
An organic cofactor that transfers electrons, atoms, or functional groups during a reaction.
Control in which a pathway’s end product reduces activity of an earlier enzyme in that pathway.
The rate measured near the start of a reaction before major substrate depletion or product accumulation.
A set of pathways that transfers energy from organic molecules to ATP through redox reactions.
Loss of electrons by an atom, ion, or molecule.
Gain of electrons by an atom, ion, or molecule.
A coupled chemical process in which one reactant is oxidized and another is reduced.
An oxidized electron carrier that accepts two electrons and one proton to form NADH.
An oxidized electron carrier that accepts two electrons and two protons to form FADH₂.
The cytosolic pathway that converts one glucose to two pyruvate, with a small net yield of ATP and NADH.
Conversion of pyruvate to acetyl-CoA, releasing carbon dioxide and reducing NAD⁺.
A cyclic mitochondrial pathway that oxidizes acetyl groups and produces carbon dioxide, reduced carriers, and ATP.
Direct formation of ATP by transferring a phosphate group from a phosphorylated substrate to ADP.
ATP production powered by electron transport and a proton gradient across a membrane.
A sequence of membrane carriers that transfers electrons through redox reactions and drives proton pumping.
Use of ion flow down an electrochemical gradient to power ATP synthesis.
Stored energy created by combined proton concentration and electrical gradients across a membrane.
A membrane enzyme that uses proton flow to phosphorylate ADP and produce ATP.
Respiration using oxygen as the final electron acceptor in an electron transport chain.
Respiration using a final electron acceptor other than oxygen in an electron transport chain.
An anaerobic pathway that regenerates NAD⁺ by transferring electrons to an organic molecule without electron transport.
Regeneration of NAD⁺ by reducing pyruvate to lactate after glycolysis.
The ratio of carbon dioxide produced to oxygen consumed during respiration.
Conversion of light energy into chemical energy stored in organic compounds, using carbon dioxide as a carbon source.
A molecule that absorbs selected wavelengths of light and can transfer excitation energy.
A green pigment whose excited electrons initiate light-dependent photosynthetic electron transfer.
A graph showing how strongly a pigment absorbs different wavelengths of light.
A graph showing the rate or effectiveness of a biological process at different light wavelengths.
A thylakoid pigment–protein complex containing an antenna and a reaction center.
Pigments and proteins that capture light energy and pass excitation to a photosystem reaction center.
The photosystem region where an excited chlorophyll transfers an electron to a primary acceptor.
Light-driven splitting of water that supplies electrons and releases protons and oxygen.
Thylakoid reactions that use light to produce ATP and reduced NADP while releasing oxygen.
Formation of ATP using a proton gradient generated by light-driven electron transport.
A cyclic set of stroma reactions that fixes carbon dioxide and produces carbohydrate precursors.
Incorporation of inorganic carbon dioxide into an organic molecule.
The five-carbon carbon-dioxide acceptor regenerated during the Calvin cycle.
The enzyme that catalyzes carbon dioxide addition to RuBP and can also react with oxygen.
The three-carbon product formed immediately after carbon dioxide fixation in the Calvin cycle.
A three-carbon sugar phosphate produced by Calvin-cycle reduction and used to build carbohydrates.
An environmental variable that restricts photosynthetic rate when it is furthest from its optimum.
A molecule that binds specifically to a receptor or other target protein.
A protein that binds a signal and initiates a cellular response.
Conversion of an external or internal signal into a sequence of cellular molecular events.
An extracellular signaling molecule that binds to a cell receptor.
A small intracellular molecule or ion that relays and often amplifies a receptor signal.
Communication by hormones carried through body fluids to target cells at distant locations.
Local communication in which a secreted signal acts on nearby target cells.
Communication in which a cell responds to a signal that it releases itself.
A signaling molecule released into circulation that regulates specific target cells bearing its receptor.
A water-soluble amino-acid polymer that usually signals through a receptor at the cell surface.
A cholesterol-derived lipid signal that commonly crosses membranes and binds an intracellular receptor.
A seven-pass membrane receptor that activates a guanine-nucleotide-binding protein after ligand binding.
A membrane receptor that activates kinase domains and phosphorylates tyrosines after ligand-induced association.
An enzyme that transfers a phosphate group from ATP to a target protein.
A sequence in which activated protein kinases phosphorylate downstream targets, relaying and amplifying a signal.
Increase in response strength when one activated component generates many active downstream molecules.
The electrical potential difference across a cell membrane caused by unequal ion distributions.
The stable negative membrane voltage of an unstimulated excitable cell.
An ATP-driven transporter that moves three sodium ions out and two potassium ions into a cell.
A membrane pore that opens or closes in response to a change in membrane voltage.
A change that makes membrane potential less negative or more positive.
Return of membrane potential toward its resting value after depolarization.
A change that makes membrane potential more negative than the resting value.
A rapid, all-or-none reversal and restoration of membrane voltage that propagates along an excitable membrane.
The membrane voltage at which regenerative opening of voltage-gated channels triggers an action potential.
A time after an action potential when another is impossible or requires a stronger stimulus.
A multilayered insulating covering around an axon that increases conduction speed.
An unmyelinated axon gap rich in voltage-gated channels where an action potential is regenerated.
Rapid propagation in which action potentials are regenerated at successive nodes of a myelinated axon.
A junction where a neuron communicates with another cell electrically or chemically.
A chemical released from a neuron that binds receptors on a postsynaptic cell.
A graded membrane-voltage change in a target cell caused by synaptic input.
The narrow extracellular gap across which neurotransmitter diffuses at a chemical synapse.
A brain region that integrates neural and endocrine control of temperature, water balance, hunger, and other functions.
An endocrine gland linked to the hypothalamus that releases hormones regulating multiple target organs.
A cluster of endocrine cells in the pancreas that secretes hormones controlling blood glucose.
A pancreatic hormone that lowers blood glucose by promoting uptake, use, and storage of glucose.
A pancreatic hormone that raises blood glucose by promoting liver glycogen breakdown and glucose production.
Formation of glycogen from glucose for storage.
Enzymatic breakdown of glycogen to release glucose units for metabolism or blood-glucose support.
An organ that filters blood, regulates fluid composition, and excretes nitrogenous wastes as urine.
vocabulary.sourceTitle: OpenStax Biology 2e, 41 Osmotic Regulation and Excretion

vocabulary.definition: The microscopic functional unit of a kidney that filters blood and modifies filtrate into urine.
vocabulary.sourceTitle: OpenStax Biology 2e, 41 Osmotic Regulation and Excretion

vocabulary.definition: A capillary tuft in a nephron where high pressure drives filtration into Bowman’s capsule.
vocabulary.sourceTitle: OpenStax Biology 2e, 41 Osmotic Regulation and Excretion

vocabulary.definition: Pressure-driven movement of water and small solutes from glomerular blood into the nephron capsule.
vocabulary.sourceTitle: OpenStax Biology 2e, 41 Osmotic Regulation and Excretion

Short-term atmospheric conditions at a particular place and time.
The statistical pattern of weather over a long period, usually decades or longer.
Warming caused when atmospheric gases absorb and re-emit infrared radiation from Earth’s surface and atmosphere.
An atmospheric gas that absorbs and emits infrared radiation at wavelengths relevant to Earth’s energy balance.
Additional warming caused by human-driven increases in atmospheric greenhouse-gas concentrations.
Long-term increase in global mean surface temperature relative to a stated reference period.
A persistent change in the statistical state of climate over decades or longer.
A change in Earth’s energy balance caused by a driver such as greenhouse gases, aerosols, or solar variation.
The fraction of incoming radiation reflected by a surface or system.
A reservoir or process that removes more carbon from the atmosphere than it releases.
A reservoir or process that releases more carbon to the atmosphere than it removes.
Capture and long-term storage of carbon in biological, geological, or engineered reservoirs.
Decline in ocean pH caused mainly by uptake of human-emitted carbon dioxide.
Increase in average sea level caused chiefly by ocean warming and loss of land ice.
Action that reduces greenhouse-gas emissions or increases removal of those gases from the atmosphere.
Adjustment to actual or expected climate effects to reduce harm or use beneficial opportunities.
A process that amplifies or dampens a climate response after an initial forcing.
Ground that remains at or below 0 °C for at least two consecutive years.
A climate-associated change in the seasonal timing of biological events such as flowering or migration.
Loss of algal symbionts or their pigments from corals under stress, leaving tissue pale and energy-limited.
